title: The Historian's Cross-Checking Process
spec_text:
The Historian's Cross-Checking Process Type: workflow **sim-id:** historians-cross-checking-process
**Library:** Mermaid
**Status:** Specified Purpose: Show, step by step, how a historian moves from a single source to a corroborated historical claim, and how bias-checking fits into that process. Bloom Taxonomy: Apply (L3) — apply the historian's questioning process to a new source. Bloom Verb: demonstrate Learning objective: Students can trace the steps a historian takes between finding a source and trusting a claim, and can name where bias-checking and corroboration occur in that process. Visual style: Mermaid flowchart, top to bottom, with decision diamonds. Steps (each is a clickable node with an infobox definition): 1. "Locate a Source" — click reveals: definition of primary/secondary source 2. "Identify Creator and Perspective" — click reveals: definition of author perspective 3. "Check for Source Bias" — click reveals: definition of source bias, with the five questions listed 4. Decision: "Does Historical Context Change the Reading?" — click reveals: definition of historical context, with the 1920s-law example 5. "Search for Corroborating Sources" — click reveals: definition of source corroboration 6. Decision: "Do Independent Sources Agree?" — Yes branch leads to "Provisional Historical Claim"; No branch leads to "Flag as Contested — Note Absent Narrative" 7. "Provisional Historical Claim" — click reveals: explanation that historical claims are always provisional, revisable with new evidence Interactivity requirement: every node is clickable via a `click` directive that opens an infobox with its definition, matching the interactivity rule for this textbook. Learner can also hover any node for a one-line tooltip preview before clicking for the full definition. Color coding: blue for source-gathering steps, yellow for decision diamonds, green for the accepted-claim outcome, red for the contested/absent-narrative outcome. Implementation: Mermaid flowchart with `click NodeId call showInfo("term")` on every node, rendered inside an iframe with a small JS shim that shows the definition text in a side panel.

title: Dominant Narrative vs. Counter-Narrative Concept Map
summary: Dominant Narrative vs. Counter-Narrative Concept Map
spec_text:
Dominant Narrative vs. Counter-Narrative Concept Map Type: infographic **sim-id:** dominant-vs-counter-narrative-map
**Library:** p5.js
**Status:** Specified Purpose: Help students see dominant narrative, counter-narrative, historical silence, and marginalization as four related — not separate — concepts. Bloom Taxonomy: Analyze (L4) — examine relationships between the four concepts. Bloom Verb: differentiate Learning objective: Given a short historical scenario, students can identify which parts represent the dominant narrative, which represent a counter-narrative, and where historical silence and marginalization are operating. Canvas layout: - Center: a node labeled "A Historical Event" - Four surrounding nodes: "Dominant Narrative," "Counter-Narrative," "Historical Silence," "Marginalization" - Connecting lines from the center to each surrounding node Visual elements: - Center node in gray - "Dominant Narrative" node in blue (larger, representing wider circulation) - "Counter-Narrative" node in orange (smaller, representing narrower circulation) - "Historical Silence" node in black with a dotted outline (representing absence) - "Marginalization" node in red, connected to both Counter-Narrative and Historical Silence with a labeled arrow reading "produces" Interactive controls: - Click any node to open an infobox with its definition and a one-sentence example drawn from the Manifest Destiny case study previewed in this chapter - Hover any connecting arrow to see a short label explaining the relationship (e.g., hovering the Marginalization→Historical Silence arrow shows: "Marginalized groups had less power to create and preserve records") Data Visibility Requirements: Stage 1: Show the four terms as unconnected labels Stage 2: On click of "A Historical Event," animate connecting lines drawing outward one at a time Stage 3: Each node click reveals its definition and example in a fixed side panel that persists as the student explores other nodes Instructional Rationale: An Analyze-level objective requires learners to see relationships, not just isolated definitions. A static list of four definitions would test Remember; a clickable concept map that surfaces the connecting arrows (with hover text) tests whether students understand how the concepts produce one another. Implementation: p5.js canvas with clickable circular nodes and a fixed-position infobox div outside the canvas that updates on click.

title: The Power Structure Pyramid
spec_text:
The Power Structure Pyramid Type: diagram **sim-id:** power-structure-pyramid
**Library:** p5.js
**Status:** Specified Purpose: Show how systemic oppression and privilege are two views of the same power structure, using a layered pyramid students can explore. Bloom Taxonomy: Understand (L2) — explain how privilege and systemic oppression relate to a shared power structure. Bloom Verb: explain Learning objective: Students can explain, in their own words, why privilege and systemic oppression are not opposites but two perspectives on the same structure. Components to show: - A pyramid divided into four horizontal bands, labeled (top to bottom): "Concentrated Authority," "Institutional Access," "Everyday Advantage/Disadvantage," "Structural Foundation (Laws, Norms, History)" - Two small figure icons that can be dragged: one labeled "Privileged Position," one labeled "Marginalized Position" Connections: A dashed vertical line connects each figure to the pyramid band it currently occupies, updating live as the figure is dragged. Interactive controls: - Drag either figure to a different vertical position on the pyramid - Clicking a pyramid band opens an infobox defining that band and giving one example connected to Chapter 1's marginalization concept - A toggle button switches the whole diagram's label set between "Privilege view" (labels describing advantage) and "Systemic oppression view" (labels describing disadvantage), so students see the same structure described from both directions Style: Flat-color pyramid, four bands in a gradient from dark (bottom/foundational) to light (top) Labels: Band names as above; figure labels "Privileged Position" / "Marginalized Position" Color scheme: Blue gradient for the pyramid bands, gold figure icon for "Privileged Position," gray figure icon for "Marginalized Position" Implementation: p5.js canvas with draggable icons snapping to the nearest band; toggle button re-labels bands via a stored label-set object.

title: From Stereotype to Discrimination — A Clickable Causal Chain
summary: From Stereotype to Discrimination — A Clickable Causal Chain
spec_text:
From Stereotype to Discrimination — A Clickable Causal Chain Type: workflow **sim-id:** stereotype-to-discrimination-chain
**Library:** Mermaid
**Status:** Specified Purpose: Let students trace, and see broken, the chain from a shared belief to a real-world outcome. Bloom Taxonomy: Analyze (L4) — differentiate between belief, attitude, and action. Bloom Verb: differentiate Learning objective: Students can place a short scenario correctly on the stereotype-to-discrimination chain and identify at which link intervention (such as anti-discrimination law) can and cannot act. Visual style: Mermaid left-to-right flowchart with four clickable nodes and one branch showing where policy intervention is possible. Nodes (each clickable with a `click` directive opening an infobox with the term's definition and a short example): 1. "Stereotype" — infobox: definition plus example ("that group is naturally good at X") 2. "Prejudice" — infobox: definition plus example (an unfavorable attitude formed before interaction) 3. "Bias" — infobox: definition, noting it can be conscious or unconscious 4. "Discrimination" — infobox: definition plus example (denial of a loan, job, or housing) Branch: a labeled arrow from "Discrimination" down to a fifth node, "Where Law Can Intervene," with an infobox explaining that anti-discrimination law targets actions and outcomes, not private beliefs — connecting back to why systemic oppression can outlast individual prejudice. Interactivity requirement: every node has a `click NodeId call showInfo("term")` directive; hovering any node shows a one-line preview tooltip before the click reveals the full infobox. Color coding: light gray for belief-stage nodes (Stereotype, Prejudice), yellow for Bias (spanning belief and institution), red for Discrimination (action/outcome), green for the "Where Law Can Intervene" node. Implementation: Mermaid flowchart with click handlers, rendered in an iframe with a JS shim providing the infobox panel.

title: Tracing a Social Construct
spec_text:
Tracing a Social Construct Type: timeline **sim-id:** tracing-a-social-construct
**Library:** vis-timeline
**Status:** Specified Purpose: Show, with a concrete documented case, how the legal category "white" changed over time in the United States — making social construction visible rather than abstract. Bloom Taxonomy: Understand (L2) — explain how a legal/social category changed over a specific historical period. Bloom Verb: explain Learning objective: Students can explain, using this specific timeline, why "race is socially constructed" is a historical claim with evidence, not just an assertion. Time period: 1790-1965 Events (each clickable, opening an infobox with detail and the primary-source type it draws on): - 1790: Naturalization Act restricts citizenship to "free white persons" — infobox explains the vagueness of "white" left undefined in law - 1840s-1850s: Irish immigrants face widespread exclusion from full "white" social status despite legal whiteness — infobox cites period cartoons and employment notices as primary sources - 1882: Chinese Exclusion Act explicitly denies naturalization to Chinese immigrants — infobox connects to nationality-based exclusion - 1923: U.S. v. Bhagat Singh Thind rules South Asian immigrants are not "white" for naturalization purposes despite some anthropological classifications of the era — infobox explains the Court's shifting rationale - 1930s-1940s: Federal housing policy (previewed here, detailed in Chapter 6) begins treating Italian and Jewish immigrants as "white" for lending purposes in ways it had not previously - 1965: Immigration and Nationality Act removes national-origin quotas, changing which groups could immigrate at all Visual style: Horizontal timeline, one row Color coding: Red markers for exclusionary legal events, green markers for inclusionary/expansion events Interactive features: Click any event for a detail panel with a one-paragraph explanation and a note on what type of primary source documents the change (statute text, court opinion, contemporary newspaper). Implementation: vis-timeline library with a JSON array of event objects, each carrying a `detail` field rendered in the panel on click.

title: The Mechanism of Land Dispossession
spec_text:
The Mechanism of Land Dispossession Type: timeline **sim-id:** mechanism-of-land-dispossession
**Library:** vis-timeline
**Status:** Specified Purpose: Connect the Indian Removal Act, the Trail of Tears, and the Homestead Act as three links in a single documented policy mechanism, not three unrelated events. Bloom Taxonomy: Analyze (L4) — examine the causal relationships connecting policy, displacement, and redistribution. Bloom Verb: examine Learning objective: Students can explain, using the specific events on this timeline, why "land dispossession" describes a connected policy mechanism rather than a series of coincidences. Time period: 1830-1862 Events (each clickable, opening an infobox with a primary-source citation type and a one-paragraph explanation): - 1830: Indian Removal Act signed — infobox notes this is the enabling legislation, citing the statute text as the primary source type - 1838-1839: Trail of Tears — infobox includes a note on documented death toll estimates and cites period military and missionary correspondence as primary sources - 1840s-1850s: Additional removals of Southeastern and Midwestern tribes under the same legal framework - 1862: Homestead Act signed — infobox explicitly connects the "public domain" land it distributes to land vacated by the prior three decades of removal, citing land office records as a primary source type Visual style: Horizontal timeline, single row, with a connecting highlighted band beneath all four events labeled "Land Dispossession Mechanism" Color coding: Red for removal/displacement events, orange for the connecting mechanism band, green for the Homestead Act redistribution event Interactive features: Clicking any event opens a detail panel; hovering the connecting band reveals a one-sentence summary of how the events link causally. Implementation: vis-timeline library with a JSON event array and a custom background band spanning the full date range.

title: Four Layers of Government Representation
spec_text:
Four Layers of Government Representation Type: graph-model **sim-id:** four-layers-of-government-representation
**Library:** vis-network
**Status:** Specified Purpose: Show tribal, local, state, and federal government as four distinct, interacting layers of representation, with tribal sovereignty positioned as independent authority rather than a subset of state government. Bloom Taxonomy: Understand (L2) — explain the relationship between tribal sovereignty and other levels of government. Bloom Verb: explain Learning objective: Students can explain why tribal nations are described as having a nation-to-nation relationship with the federal government, rather than being classified under state or local government. Node types: 1. Federal Government (large blue circle, center-top) 2. State Government (medium orange circle) 3. Local Government (small orange circle, connected to State) 4. Tribal Nation (medium green circle, connected directly to Federal, NOT to State) — properties: name (example tribal nation used for illustration), governing authority, treaty status Edge types: 1. "Constitutional Authority" (solid black arrow, Federal → State) 2. "Delegated Authority" (solid black arrow, State → Local) 3. "Nation-to-Nation Relationship" (double-headed solid green arrow, Federal ↔ Tribal Nation) — distinct styling from the other edges to visually reinforce that this is not a delegation relationship 4. "Consultation Requirement" (dashed green arrow, Tribal Nation → State, labeled with a note that this is a limited, specific-purpose relationship, not general authority) Layout: Hierarchical, with Tribal Nation positioned at the same vertical level as State Government but visually separated to the side, connected upward directly to Federal Interactive features: - Hover any node: show its properties in a tooltip - Click any node: highlight all its direct connections and open a side panel with the node's full definition - Click the "Nation-to-Nation Relationship" edge: open an infobox explaining why this relationship is legally and historically distinct from federal-state or state-local delegation Legend: Node color key (blue = federal, orange = state/local, green = tribal) and edge style key (solid = direct authority, dashed = limited/specific relationship) Implementation: vis-network with a hierarchical layout option disabled for the Tribal Nation node's horizontal position (custom fixed positioning) so it renders beside, not beneath, State Government.

title: A Redlined Map, Then and Now
summary: A Redlined Map, Then and Now
spec_text:
A Redlined Map, Then and Now Type: map **sim-id:** redlined-map-then-and-now
**Library:** Leaflet
**Status:** Specified Purpose: Let students overlay a historical Home Owners' Loan Corporation redlining map with present-day data (e.g., median home value or tree canopy coverage) for the same city, to see redlining's decades-long effect made visible. Bloom Taxonomy: Analyze (L4) — examine the relationship between a historical policy map and present-day outcomes. Bloom Verb: examine Learning objective: Given a historical redlining map and a present-day data layer for the same city, students can identify the correlation between historical grade and current outcome, and explain at least one mechanism (access to credit) connecting the two. Geographic scope: A single representative U.S. city (implementation note: use a city with well-documented, publicly available HOLC map data, such as Minneapolis or St. Paul, Minnesota, to connect directly to the course's Minnesota standards) Locations: Neighborhood polygons color-coded by original 1930s HOLC grade (A=green, B=blue, C=yellow, D=red, matching the original historical color scheme) Data flows: N/A (this is a layered map, not a flow map) Interactive controls: - Opacity slider to blend the historical grade layer with a present-day data layer - Toggle to switch the present-day layer between two datasets (e.g., median home value, tree canopy percentage) - Click any neighborhood polygon to open an infobox showing its 1930s grade, the original HOLC surveyor's stated rationale (drawn from the historical record), and its current value for the selected present-day dataset Labels: HOLC grade legend (A/B/C/D), present-day dataset legend Color scheme: Original HOLC four-color scale for the historical layer; a separate sequential color scale (e.g., light-to-dark blue) for whichever present-day dataset is selected Interactive features: hover for a quick tooltip (grade + current value), click for the full infobox with historical rationale text Implementation: Leaflet.js with two GeoJSON layers (historical HOLC polygons, present-day data polygons) and a blend/opacity control.

title: The Compounding Chain of Economic Exclusion
summary: The Compounding Chain of Economic Exclusion
spec_text:
The Compounding Chain of Economic Exclusion Type: workflow **sim-id:** compounding-chain-of-economic-exclusion
**Library:** Mermaid
**Status:** Specified Purpose: Let students trace the full documented chain from a single 1930s policy (redlining) through to a present-day wealth gap, and evaluate where a reparations proposal could intervene. Bloom Taxonomy: Evaluate (L5) — judge the effectiveness of proposed interventions at different points in a documented causal chain. Bloom Verb: justify Learning objective: Given the compounding chain from redlining to wealth gap, students can identify at least two points where policy intervention (including reparations) could act, and justify which point would have the largest measurable effect. Visual style: Mermaid top-to-bottom flowchart with clickable nodes and one branch showing possible intervention points. Nodes (each clickable with a `click` directive opening an infobox): 1. "Redlining (1930s)" — infobox: definition and historical dates 2. "Housing Discrimination" — infobox: definition, notes continuation after 1968 3. "Reduced Access to Credit" — infobox: definition and mechanism 4. "Community Disinvestment" — infobox: definition 5. "Wealth Gap (Present Day)" — infobox: definition, notes wealth vs. income distinction 6. Branch node: "Possible Interventions" connected to nodes 2, 3, and 5 with dashed arrows, each labeled with a real policy category (fair housing enforcement, credit access programs, reparations) — infobox on each dashed arrow explains what that intervention targets and at which point in the chain Interactivity requirement: every node and every labeled intervention arrow has a `click` directive opening an infobox; hovering any node shows a preview tooltip. Color coding: red for the originating policy node, orange for the mechanism nodes, dark red for the present-day outcome node, green for the intervention branch. Implementation: Mermaid flowchart with click handlers on nodes and edges, rendered in an iframe with a JS shim for the infobox panel.

title: Policing History Timeline
spec_text:
Policing History Timeline Type: timeline **sim-id:** policing-history-timeline
**Library:** vis-timeline
**Status:** Specified Purpose: Show the documented institutional evolution of American policing, providing historical context for later sections on selective enforcement and racial profiling. Bloom Taxonomy: Understand (L2) — summarize the major institutional shifts in the history of American policing. Bloom Verb: summarize Learning objective: Students can summarize at least three major institutional shifts in the history of American policing and explain why this history is treated as historical context (Chapter 1) for evaluating present-day enforcement patterns. Time period: 1700s-present Events (each clickable with an infobox citing the type of historical source involved): - 1700s-1865: Slave patrols in Southern colonies and states — infobox notes these as among the earliest organized policing institutions in the region, citing state slave-code statutes as a primary source type - 1838-1900s: Formation of professional municipal police departments (Boston 1838 cited as an early example) — infobox notes the primarily order-maintenance and property-protection origins of these forces - 1960s-1970s: Civil rights era confrontations between police and protesters, widely documented on film and in news photography - 1970s-1990s: "War on drugs" era policy shifts and their connection to sentencing policy (previewed here, detailed later in this chapter) - 1990s-2000s: Rise of "broken windows" and zero-tolerance policing strategies - 2010s-present: Body camera adoption and community policing reform efforts following widely documented incidents Visual style: Horizontal timeline, single row, grouped into shaded eras Color coding: distinct background shading per era (colonial/slave-patrol era, professionalization era, civil rights era, war-on-drugs era, reform era) Interactive features: click any event for a detail panel; hover for one-line preview. Implementation: vis-timeline library with era-grouping background bands and a JSON event dataset.

title: Same Event, Two Frames
spec_text:
Same Event, Two Frames Type: infographic **sim-id:** same-event-two-frames
**Library:** p5.js
**Status:** Specified Purpose: Show two side-by-side, entirely factual headline-and-lead-paragraph pairs describing the same hypothetical event, differing only in framing choices, so students can see the framing effect operating without any factual falsehood present. Bloom Taxonomy: Analyze (L4) — differentiate between factual content and framing choices in a news text. Bloom Verb: differentiate Learning objective: Given two framings of the same factual event, students can identify the specific word choices, ordering, and visual choices producing the different impressions, without identifying either version as factually false. Canvas layout: - Two side-by-side panels, each showing a headline, a one-paragraph lead, and a representative image placeholder - Below both panels, a highlighted-differences toggle Interactive controls: - Toggle: "Highlight Word Choice Differences" — underlines the specific words that differ in emotional register between the two panels (e.g., "protesters" vs. "mob," "official" vs. "operative") - Click any highlighted word pair: infobox explains the connotation difference and cites this as the framing effect, not factual inaccuracy - Toggle: "Show Fact-Check" — a checkmark confirms both versions report the same underlying verifiable facts Data Visibility Requirements: Stage 1: Show both panels unhighlighted, prompting the student to spot differences on their own first Stage 2: On toggle, reveal highlighted word-choice differences Stage 3: On second toggle, confirm both are factually accurate, isolating framing as the sole variable Instructional Rationale: An Analyze-level framing objective requires students to separate two things usually experienced together — factual content and framing choice. Presenting two factually verified panels side-by-side, with an explicit fact-check confirmation, is necessary because students otherwise default to treating "differently framed" as synonymous with "one side lying." Implementation: p5.js or HTML/CSS panel layout with a JS toggle that applies/removes highlight spans on pre-marked text.

title: Minnesota Tribal Nations Map
spec_text:
Minnesota Tribal Nations Map Type: map **sim-id:** minnesota-tribal-nations-map
**Library:** Leaflet
**Status:** Specified Purpose: Show the location and identity of Minnesota's eleven federally recognized tribal nations, each as a distinct, named sovereign government rather than an undifferentiated category. Bloom Taxonomy: Remember (L1) — identify Minnesota's tribal nations and their locations. Bloom Verb: identify Learning objective: Students can identify, by name and general location, the tribal nations with reservations or trust land in Minnesota, and distinguish Dakota from Ojibwe (Anishinaabe) nations among them. Geographic scope: State of Minnesota Locations: Reservation and trust-land boundaries for each of the eleven federally recognized tribal nations in Minnesota, color-coded by nation (Ojibwe nations in one color family, Dakota nations in a distinct color family) Data flows: N/A (boundary map, not a flow map) Labels: Each nation's name in both its own language and common English usage, displayed on click Legend: Color key distinguishing Ojibwe and Dakota nations; note explaining that boundary size on the map reflects present-day reservation and trust land, not historical territory (a distinction the infobox for each nation makes explicit, connecting to Chapter 4's land dispossession content) Interactive features: - Click any tribal nation's territory: opens an infobox with the nation's name, language family, tribal government structure, and a link-style reference to its official government website (described, not hyperlinked directly, for specification purposes) - Toggle: "Show Historical Territory" overlay, contrasting present-day reservation boundaries with the much larger documented historical territory, reinforcing the land dispossession concept from Chapter 4 Implementation: Leaflet.js with a GeoJSON layer of tribal boundaries and a toggle-able historical-territory GeoJSON overlay.

title: Diffusion Model Comparator
spec_text:
Diffusion Model Comparator Type: graph-model **sim-id:** diffusion-model-comparator
**Library:** vis-network
**Status:** Specified Purpose: Let students compare expansion diffusion and relocation diffusion using the same starting scenario, to see how the diffusion model chosen changes the interpretation of a historical spread of culture. Bloom Taxonomy: Analyze (L4) — differentiate between diffusion models applied to the same historical scenario. Bloom Verb: differentiate Learning objective: Given a single historical example of a cultural practice spreading between regions, students can classify the spread as primarily expansion diffusion, relocation diffusion, or a mix of both, and justify the classification. Node types: 1. Origin Region (green circle) — properties: name, cultural practice of interest 2. Destination Region (blue circle) — properties: name, degree of adoption Edge types: 1. "Expansion Diffusion" (solid arrow, origin retains full practice while destination adopts it) — clicking shows an infobox with a worked historical example 2. "Relocation Diffusion" (dashed arrow, showing population movement carrying the practice, with reduced presence remaining at origin) — clicking shows a worked historical example Layout: Two side-by-side mini-diagrams (one per diffusion type), sharing the same origin/destination region pair for direct comparison Interactive features: - Toggle between three preset historical scenarios (a trade-driven example, a migration-driven example, and a conquest-driven example) - For each scenario, click either edge type to see whether it fits, with a written justification - A "Which model fits best?" quiz prompt at the bottom, with a short-answer text box (not auto-graded, intended for classroom discussion) Implementation: vis-network with two small fixed two-node graphs side by side, and a scenario-switching control that updates the node/edge metadata and infobox content.

title: Global Migration Pattern Map
spec_text:
Global Migration Pattern Map Type: map **sim-id:** global-migration-pattern-map
**Library:** Leaflet
**Status:** Specified Purpose: Show major documented global migration flows over a defined recent period, connecting each flow's stated causes to concepts from this chapter (forced migration, U.S. foreign policy, border formation). Bloom Taxonomy: Analyze (L4) — examine the relationship between documented causes and resulting migration flows. Bloom Verb: examine Learning objective: Students can select a major migration flow on the map and correctly attribute it to one or more of this chapter's named causal mechanisms, using cited documentation. Geographic scope: World map Locations: Origin and destination regions for 5-6 major, well-documented late-20th/21st-century migration flows Data flows (arrows): Curved directional arrows sized by relative magnitude, colored by primary documented cause (forced migration due to conflict = red, economic pressure = orange, environmental displacement = green) Labels: Region names, arrow magnitude legend Interactive features: - Click any flow arrow: infobox with the flow's documented primary and contributing causes, citing the type of source (UN refugee agency reports, government migration statistics) used to establish the data - Filter checkboxes to show/hide flows by primary cause category Legend: Cause-category color key, arrow-width magnitude key Implementation: Leaflet.js with curved polyline arrows (using a curve-generating utility) and a filterable dataset of flow objects.

title: Strategy Toolkit — Choosing a Social Movement Tactic
summary: Strategy Toolkit — Choosing a Social Movement Tactic
spec_text:
Strategy Toolkit — Choosing a Social Movement Tactic Type: microsim **sim-id:** strategy-toolkit-social-movement-tactic
**Library:** p5.js
**Status:** Specified Purpose: Let students select a specific historical scenario and choose among strategy options, then compare their choice to what movement organizers actually chose and why. Bloom Taxonomy: Apply (L3) — apply social movement strategy concepts to a specific scenario. Bloom Verb: apply Learning objective: Given a scenario describing a movement's goal, resources, and political environment, students can select an appropriate strategic mix (from nonviolent resistance, civil disobedience, grassroots organizing, litigation, electoral organizing) and compare their reasoning to the documented historical choice. Canvas layout: - Left (350px): scenario description panel with a dropdown to select among 3 preset historical scenarios (e.g., a voting-rights campaign, a workplace-organizing campaign, a marriage-equality legal campaign) - Right (350px): five strategy option cards the student can select (multiple selections allowed, since real movements combine strategies) Interactive controls: - Scenario dropdown - Strategy card multi-select (click to toggle selection) - "Compare to Historical Record" button Data Visibility Requirements: Stage 1: Scenario description shown, no strategy selected Stage 2: Student selects one or more strategy cards Stage 3: On comparison, show which strategies the actual historical movement used (from documented sources), with a brief explanation of why, and note any strategies the student selected that were NOT historically used, with an explanation of the tradeoff Instructional Rationale: An Apply-level objective benefits from a low-stakes, comparison-based structure — letting students commit to a strategic choice before revealing the documented historical answer preserves the cognitive work of application, rather than turning the exercise into simple lookup. Default parameters: no scenario selected at load Implementation: p5.js canvas with dropdown and toggle-card UI elements; a small local dataset of three scenario objects, each with a documented-strategy answer key and explanation text.

title: From Slavery to Desegregation — A Traceable Chain
summary: From Slavery to Desegregation — A Traceable Chain
spec_text:
From Slavery to Desegregation — A Traceable Chain Type: timeline **sim-id:** slavery-to-desegregation-chain
**Library:** vis-timeline
**Status:** Specified Purpose: Connect the legacy of slavery, Reconstruction, Jim Crow, and desegregation as a single traceable chain, emphasizing that Jim Crow was an active reversal of Reconstruction-era gains rather than a simple continuation of the status quo. Bloom Taxonomy: Understand (L2) — summarize the causal chain connecting four historical periods. Bloom Verb: summarize Learning objective: Students can summarize why Jim Crow is best understood as a documented reversal of specific Reconstruction-era gains, not merely an unbroken continuation of slavery-era conditions. Time period: 1865-1968 Events (each clickable with an infobox citing primary-source type): - 1865: 13th Amendment ratified, formally abolishing slavery — infobox notes the "legacy of slavery" concept persisting despite formal abolition - 1865-1877: Reconstruction era — infobox lists specific documented gains (Black elected officials, 14th and 15th Amendments) with a note on federal troop withdrawal in 1877 as the era's end - 1877-1950s: Jim Crow era — infobox explicitly frames this as a reversal, citing specific segregation statutes as primary-source examples - 1954: Brown v. Board of Education — infobox cites the Supreme Court opinion as a primary source - 1955-1968: Civil rights movement peak organizing period — infobox connects to nonviolent resistance and grassroots organizing concepts - 1964-1965: Civil Rights Act and Voting Rights Act — infobox cites statute text Visual style: Horizontal timeline, single row, with a shaded background band explicitly labeled "Reversal Period" over the Jim Crow era to visually reinforce the reversal framing Color coding: gray for the slavery-legacy starting point, green for Reconstruction gains, red for the Jim Crow reversal band, blue for the desegregation resolution events Interactive features: click any event for detail panel; hover the "Reversal Period" band for a one-sentence summary of what specifically was reversed. Implementation: vis-timeline with a custom background band and a JSON event dataset.

title: Shared Origins, Divergent Paths
spec_text:
Shared Origins, Divergent Paths Type: timeline **sim-id:** shared-origins-divergent-paths
**Library:** vis-timeline
**Status:** Specified Purpose: Show the chronological and historical relationship among Judaism, Christianity, and Islam without asserting the truth of any tradition's theological claims — a strictly historical-chronology presentation. Bloom Taxonomy: Understand (L2) — explain the historical and chronological relationship among three related traditions. Bloom Verb: explain Learning objective: Students can explain, using only historically documented dates and events, why Judaism, Christianity, and Islam are described as sharing a common lineage while remaining theologically distinct. Time period: circa 1800 BCE - 700 CE Events (each clickable with an infobox strictly limited to historical/documentary framing, not theological claims): - circa 1800 BCE: Traditional dating of the patriarch Abraham, shared ancestral figure across all three traditions - circa 1200 BCE: Traditional dating of the Israelite exodus narrative and early Judaism's formation - circa 30 CE: Life and teachings of Jesus of Nazareth, within the context of Second Temple Judaism - circa 100 CE: Growing distinction between Christianity and Judaism as separate religious communities - 610-632 CE: Prophetic career of Muhammad in Mecca and Medina - 632 CE onward: Early spread of Islam across the Arabian Peninsula and beyond Visual style: Horizontal timeline, single row, with three colored bands beneath showing the approximate span of each tradition's distinct identity (Judaism spanning the full timeline, Christianity beginning ~100 CE, Islam beginning ~632 CE) Color coding: one distinct color per tradition's band, applied consistently Interactive features: click any event for a strictly historical detail panel (citing archaeological, textual, or historiographical sources as the source type); hover any band for a one-line description of that tradition's historical continuity. Implementation: vis-timeline with three background bands and a JSON event dataset; all infobox text reviewed for strictly historical (not theological) framing.

title: Suppression and Revitalization as Mirror Processes
summary: Suppression and Revitalization as Mirror Processes
spec_text:
Suppression and Revitalization as Mirror Processes Type: workflow **sim-id:** suppression-and-revitalization-mirror
**Library:** Mermaid
**Status:** Specified Purpose: Show linguistic suppression and language revitalization as mirror-image processes acting on the same underlying resource — a community's language — in opposite directions. Bloom Taxonomy: Understand (L2) — explain the relationship between a suppression policy and a later revitalization effort. Bloom Verb: explain Learning objective: Students can explain why language revitalization is described as a direct response to a specific, prior linguistic suppression policy, rather than a spontaneous, unrelated cultural trend. Visual style: Mermaid diagram with two parallel horizontal tracks, one above the other, connected by vertical linking arrows at matched stages Nodes, Suppression track (top, left to right, each clickable): 1. "Policy Decision (e.g., boarding school language ban)" 2. "Reduced Intergenerational Transmission" 3. "Language Endangerment" Nodes, Revitalization track (bottom, left to right, each clickable): 1. "Community Organizing (connects to grassroots organizing, Chapter 11)" 2. "Elder-Youth Documentation Partnerships" 3. "Renewed Intergenerational Transmission" Linking arrows: dashed vertical arrows connecting "Language Endangerment" (top) to "Community Organizing" (bottom), labeled "Motivates Response," and connecting "Renewed Intergenerational Transmission" (bottom) back up to a new node "Partial Recovery," visually closing the loop Interactivity requirement: every node has a `click` directive opening an infobox with its definition and a real-world example category (without asserting a single specific tribe's data, described generically as "a documented case" per specification guidance) Color coding: red for the suppression track, green for the revitalization track, gray dashed for linking arrows Implementation: Mermaid flowchart with two subgraphs (top and bottom tracks) and click handlers on every node.

title: Triangulating Three Source Types
spec_text:
Triangulating Three Source Types Type: diagram **sim-id:** triangulating-three-source-types
**Library:** p5.js
**Status:** Specified Purpose: Let students practice source triangulation using a worked example with a government record, a newspaper account, and an oral history excerpt describing the same local event, to see where the three converge and where one adds information the others lack. Bloom Taxonomy: Apply (L3) — apply source triangulation to a worked example. Bloom Verb: apply Learning objective: Given three short source excerpts (a government record, a newspaper account, and an oral history excerpt) describing the same illustrative local event, students can identify specific claims that all three sources agree on, and specific claims found in only one source, and explain what that gap suggests about the historical record. Components to show: - Three labeled source panels arranged in a triangle: "Government Record," "Newspaper Account," "Oral History Excerpt" - A center "Convergence Zone" area Connections: draggable claim tags (short factual statements extracted from each source) that students drag into the center Convergence Zone if they believe the claim is supported by multiple sources, or leave at their originating panel if supported by only one Interactive controls: - Drag claim tags between panels and the center zone - "Check Triangulation" button reveals which claims are genuinely corroborated across sources and which are unique to a single source type, with a note on why the unique claims matter (often the oral history excerpt contains detail absent from official records — precisely the kind of detail this course has asked you to seek out) Style: Triangular layout with three source panels and a center convergence zone Labels: source-type panel headers, claim tag text Color scheme: one color per source type panel, with the convergence zone in a neutral background color Implementation: p5.js canvas with draggable text-tag objects and defined drop-zone regions; a small worked-example dataset of claim tags with correct-convergence metadata.
